index.add_items(np.random.rand(n_elements, dim).astype('float32'))

# Query: ef controls recall/speed tradeoff
index.set_ef(50)  # ef must be >= k
query = np.random.rand(1, dim).astype('float32')
labels, distances = index.knn_query(query, k=10)
print(f'Top-10 neighbours: {labels[0]}')

words.etymology: HNSW stands for Hierarchical Navigable Small World. 'Small world' references the Watts-Strogatz small-world network model (1998); 'Navigable' means the graph topology supports greedy routing to any target; 'Hierarchical' refers to the layered structure added by Malkov and Yashunin.

words.shortDefinition: A database that bills per query rather than per provisioned instance, scaling compute to zero when idle.
words.simpleDefinition: A serverless database decouples billing from provisioned capacity: you pay for queries executed or CPU-seconds consumed, not for an always-on instance. Compute scales to zero when idle and resumes within seconds on the next request. This makes it economical for applications with sporadic or unpredictable traffic patterns — the classic case being development databases and preview environments.
words.longDefinition: Serverless databases extend the serverless computing model (AWS Lambda, 2014) to persistent data stores. The defining characteristics: billing per request or per compute-second (not per provisioned instance), automatic scale-to-zero when idle, and automatic scale-up on traffic spikes — all transparent to the application. The engineering challenge is substantial: traditional RDBMS engines require tens of seconds to start (process initialization, WAL recovery, connection warm-up), which makes true scale-to-zero unusable. The architectures that enable serverless databases are precisely those with compute-storage separation: because all durable state lives in the storage layer, the compute layer can be destroyed and recreated in milliseconds without data loss or recovery time. Aurora Serverless v2 (2022) scales in 0.5 ACU (Aurora Capacity Unit) increments every few seconds, adjusting to workload without cold start — but it does not scale to zero (minimum 0.5 ACU). Aurora Serverless v1 (2018) scaled to zero but had a 30–60 second cold start. Neon scales to zero with ~500 ms cold start because the stateless compute process restarts immediately and the storage layer is always warm. CockroachDB Serverless (2021) provisions shared compute clusters and gives each tenant a virtual cluster — scale-to-zero per tenant without the overhead of a fully isolated compute node. PlanetScale (MySQL, 2022) charges per row read/written. The connection pooling challenge (Postgres opens a heavyweight process per connection, incompatible with thousands of transient serverless clients) is universally solved with a connection pooler layer: RDS Proxy (Aurora), PgBouncer (Neon), Vitess vtgate (PlanetScale). By 2026, serverless databases are the default choice for side projects, preview environments, and applications with unpredictable traffic — the economics are compelling for everything except steady high-throughput workloads.
words.connector: Think of a serverless database like pay-per-use electricity at a vacation cabin: when you're not there, nothing runs and you're not billed; when you arrive and flip a switch, power comes on within seconds. A traditional provisioned database is like keeping the lights on all year just in case you visit.
words.techContext: The team's 200 PR preview environments each connected to a dedicated Neon serverless branch; total storage cost was $8/month because each branch paid only for pages that diverged from the parent, and idle compute scaled to zero between CI runs.
words.exampleSentence: Switching development databases to serverless reduced their monthly bill by 85% because the databases scaled to zero after business hours, compared to 24/7 provisioned RDS instances that sat at 2% CPU utilization overnight.
words.etymology: Serverless is a marketing misnomer — servers exist, but they are abstracted from the customer. The term entered mainstream usage with AWS Lambda (2014); 'serverless database' was popularized by Aurora Serverless (2018) and Neon (2022) to mean a database where compute capacity is not provisioned or managed by the user.

words.shortDefinition: A topology with no designated primary; writes go to a quorum of nodes and are reconciled by anti-entropy.
words.simpleDefinition: In leaderless replication, any node in the cluster can accept writes and reads. Writes are sent to W of N nodes; reads are sent to R of N nodes. As long as W + R > N, a read quorum always overlaps a write quorum, ensuring readers see the latest write. When nodes fall behind, an anti-entropy process detects and repairs divergence. Cassandra and Riak use this model.
words.longDefinition: Leaderless replication (popularized by Amazon's Dynamo paper, DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007) eliminates the single leader that is the bottleneck and single point of failure in primary-replica topologies. Every node is equal; any node can receive any read or write. Quorum reads and writes provide configurable consistency: with replication factor N, a write to W nodes and a read from R nodes satisfies W + R > N, guaranteeing that at least one node in any read quorum has seen the latest write. Tuning W and R lets operators trade consistency for availability per-operation: W=1 maximizes write availability; R=N maximizes read consistency. The trade-offs: eventual consistency with tunable quorums (even with W + R > N, there are edge cases — a stale read can occur if a write reached W nodes but not the R nodes chosen for the next read in a concurrent window). Anti-entropy ensures nodes eventually converge: Cassandra uses a Merkle tree comparison between nodes (repair process) to detect and fix divergence; Dynamo uses a gossip protocol and anti-entropy background sync. Conflict resolution when two writes reach different quorums simultaneously: last-write-wins (LWW) with client-generated timestamps is the simplest but can silently discard concurrent writes; vector clocks (Riak) detect concurrent writes and present both to the application or a merge function; CRDTs make conflict resolution automatic for supported data types. Sloppy quorums extend availability during partitions: writes that cannot reach the required quorum are accepted by available nodes with a hint that they should be forwarded to the real owner when it recovers (hinted handoff). In 2026, leaderless replication is the standard model for Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak, and the Apache Cassandra-compatible services (Amazon Keyspaces, Azure Managed Instance for Apache Cassandra).
words.connector: Think of leaderless replication like a jury without a foreperson: every juror's vote counts, decisions require a majority (quorum), and if a juror was absent during deliberation, they get briefed afterward (anti-entropy repair) so the record is eventually consistent.
words.techContext: The team configured Cassandra with RF=3, W=2, R=2 (quorum) for strong consistency on payment records, while using W=1, R=1 for user session data where slightly stale reads were acceptable in exchange for lower write latency.
words.exampleSentence: Leaderless replication with sloppy quorums allowed the Cassandra cluster to continue accepting writes during the datacenter network partition, with hinted handoff delivering the buffered writes to the isolated nodes when connectivity was restored.
words.etymology: Leaderless describes the absence of a designated primary node; the pattern was described (without this name) in Amazon's Dynamo paper (DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007) and in Werner Vogels's blog posts on 'eventually consistent' storage; the term 'leaderless replication' was popularized by Martin Kleppmann in 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications' (2017).

words.shortDefinition: A distributed commit protocol that embeds Paxos consensus per-shard to tolerate coordinator failures, unlike vanilla 2PC.
words.simpleDefinition: Paxos commit (Gray and Lamport, 2004) replaces the single coordinator of 2PC with a separate Paxos consensus group for each participant's prepare vote. Because each participant's decision is stored in a replicated Paxos log rather than on a single coordinator, any node that reads all the Paxos logs can determine the transaction outcome — the coordinator is no longer a single point of blocking failure.
words.longDefinition: Gray and Lamport, 'Consensus on Transaction Commit' (2004) identified 2PC's fundamental weakness: the coordinator holds the commit decision in one place, so coordinator failure blocks all participants indefinitely. Their solution: run one Paxos instance per participant to record that participant's prepare vote in a replicated log. Classic 2PC has one coordinator making a binary decision (commit or abort). Paxos commit has one Paxos instance per participant (e.g., Paxos_A, Paxos_B, Paxos_C for three participants), each running among the same acceptor group (typically 2f+1 nodes for f failure tolerance). Each participant is the leader proposer for its own Paxos instance. The overall transaction commits if and only if all participant Paxos instances chose PREPARED. The key property: any acceptor node that has learned the results of all N participant Paxos instances can determine the overall transaction outcome with no coordinator involvement. If the leader of one Paxos instance fails, any other acceptor can take over as proposer and drive that instance to completion using standard Paxos recovery. Message complexity: 2PC requires 2 round trips; Paxos commit requires 3–5 message delays (Paxos Phase 1 + Phase 2 + learn), but with no single blocking point. Google Spanner's distributed transaction protocol is a direct implementation: each shard's Raft group (a multi-Paxos log) serves as the acceptor group for that shard's prepare vote. The transaction coordinator distributes prepare requests across shard leaders; each shard leader runs a Raft log entry for its vote. Any surviving majority in each Raft group can recover the shard's vote after coordinator failure, unblocking the transaction. The Gray-Lamport paper formally proves non-blocking: as long as a majority of acceptors in each instance are available, the protocol terminates — in sharp contrast to 2PC (coordinator failure → indefinite blocking) and 3PC (safe only under crash failures, not network partitions).
words.connector: Think of Paxos commit like replacing the single notary who validates a multi-party contract with a panel of notaries for each signer — even if the original notary (coordinator) disappears, any panel can certify their signer's decision and the overall contract can proceed to conclusion.
words.techContext: Spanner's use of Paxos commit means that a coordinator process failure during a distributed transaction does not block participating shards — each shard's Raft group independently holds its vote and can be recovered by any surviving replica without human intervention.
words.exampleSentence: Paxos commit eliminated the coordinator-failure blocking problem that had caused 30-second lock storms in the team's previous 2PC implementation, since any Spanner shard replica could recover its local vote log and resume the transaction.
words.etymology: Paxos Commit combines the Paxos consensus algorithm (Lamport 1998) with the two-phase commit protocol (Jim Gray 1978). The protocol was proposed by Jim Gray and Leslie Lamport in 'Consensus on Transaction Commit' (ACM Transactions on Database Systems, 2006, based on a 2004 technical report).

words.shortDefinition: A stronger-than-serializable guarantee: if transaction T2 starts after T1 commits in real time, T2 sees T1's writes.
words.simpleDefinition: External consistency (also called strict serializability or linearizability at the transaction level) adds a real-world time constraint to serializability: if transaction T1 commits, and then T2 starts after T1 commits in wall-clock time, T2 must see T1's effects. Spanner achieves this by assigning commit timestamps using TrueTime and delaying commit until the clock uncertainty window clears.
words.longDefinition: Serializability guarantees that the execution of concurrent transactions appears equivalent to some serial order — but it makes no claim about which serial order. Clients observing the system from the outside could see orders that contradict real-world causality: T1 might commit at 12:00:00, T2 starts at 12:00:01, yet T2 could read a snapshot that does not include T1's writes if the serialization order places T1 after T2. External consistency (Lampson and Sturgis 1976; called 'external consistency' in the Spanner paper) rules this out: the serialization order must agree with the real-world (wall-clock) order of transactions. If T2 starts after T1 commits in real time, T2's serial order position must come after T1's. This is equivalent to linearizability applied at the transaction level — also called strict serializability. Spanner achieves external consistency via the commit-wait protocol: the transaction coordinator picks a commit timestamp s = TT.now().latest (the upper bound of the current TrueTime interval), executes the distributed Paxos-based 2PC across involved shards, writes the commit record with timestamp s, then waits until TT.after(s) is true (i.e., until TT.now().earliest > s). This wait — approximately 2ε ≈ 14 ms at typical Google datacenter clock accuracy — guarantees that any future TT.now() call on any node returns a earliest > s, so any transaction that starts after this commit will receive a start timestamp > s and must see this transaction's writes. Read-only transactions can use a past timestamp outside the uncertainty window and skip commit-wait entirely, executing at full speed. External consistency dramatically simplifies distributed application reasoning — clients can rely on the database's ordering agreeing with the real world — at the cost of ~14 ms added write latency. Spanner is the only globally distributed production database that delivers this guarantee at scale as of 2026.
words.connector: Think of external consistency like a timestamp requirement for legal contracts: a contract signed at 3pm is legally after any contract signed at 2pm, and anyone reading legal records after 3pm will see both contracts — the timestamps create a binding causal chain that reflects the real world.
words.techContext: Spanner's external consistency guarantee meant the financial application could transfer funds in one transaction and immediately read the updated balance in the next transaction from any global region, with no stale-read surprises.
words.exampleSentence: External consistency in Spanner meant that a payment confirmed to the user was guaranteed to be visible in every subsequent balance inquiry, regardless of which global region served the read — eliminating the class of 'payment shows as pending' bugs the team had fought with eventually consistent databases.
words.etymology: External consistency was defined by Lampson and Sturgis in 'Crash Recovery in a Distributed Data Storage System' (1976 Xerox PARC report). The term was re-introduced to mainstream database literature by the Spanner paper (Corbett et al., OSDI 2012), which used it to describe a guarantee stronger than serialisability — one that respects real-world time ordering.

words.shortDefinition: A query engine processing column batches with SIMD in tight loops; DuckDB and ClickHouse are canonical examples.
words.simpleDefinition: A vectorised columnar engine combines two complementary optimizations: columnar storage (keeping each column's values contiguous on disk and in memory) and vectorised execution (processing batches of 1,024–8,192 values per operator call rather than one row at a time). Together, they maximize CPU cache utilization, enable SIMD auto-vectorisation, and can sustain analytical throughput of billions of rows per second.
words.longDefinition: Vectorised columnar execution is the dominant paradigm for analytical database engines as of 2026. It builds on two independently valuable ideas that compound when combined. Columnar storage (the Decomposition Storage Model, DSM) stores each column's values as a contiguous array rather than interleaving columns within rows. For an analytical query that sums one column of a 100-column table, DSM reads 1/100th of the data that row storage (NSM) reads. Vectorised execution (MonetDB/X100, Boncz, Zukowski, and Nes, CIDR 2005) processes batches of values per operator call rather than one row at a time. A batch of int64 values in a contiguous array can be processed with AVX-512 instructions that handle 8 values per CPU cycle. The tight inner loop over a vector of fixed-type values is highly amenable to loop unrolling, SIMD auto-vectorisation by the compiler, and CPU branch prediction. Typical SIMD speedup over scalar: 4–16× for arithmetic operations. The combination: columnar storage ensures the values reaching the CPU are densely packed (no column skipping, good cache line utilization), and vectorised execution turns each cache-line load into SIMD-parallel work. Additional optimizations in modern engines: late materialisation (apply predicates on individual columns before assembling full rows, reducing data movement), dictionary encoding (replace high-cardinality string columns with integer codes, enabling integer SIMD comparisons on string predicates), and zone maps (skip entire column chunks where min/max bounds exclude the query predicate). Production engines: DuckDB (embedded, push-based, Apache Arrow native), ClickHouse (distributed, MergeTree storage), Apache Velox (Facebook's open-source C++ vectorised execution library used in Presto and Spark), and Databricks Photon (a vectorised C++ replacement for Apache Spark's Java-based execution engine that delivers 3–10× speedup on Parquet workloads).
words.connector: Think of a vectorised columnar engine like a car wash assembly line: instead of washing one car at a time from hood to trunk (row-at-a-time), the line simultaneously runs every car's hood section through the first station, then every roof, then every trunk — operating on all cars' same part at once (column batch), which lets specialised robots run in parallel.
words.techContext: Databricks Photon's vectorised columnar execution processed the team's 10 TB Parquet dataset aggregation in 4 minutes instead of 35 minutes with the standard Spark JVM engine, while consuming 40% fewer compute-hours due to reduced CPU overhead per row.
words.exampleSentence: The vectorised columnar engine scanned 2.3 billion event rows in 1.8 seconds on eight cores by processing 4,096-value AVX-512 SIMD batches over a compressed int32 column, achieving effective throughput of 1.3 billion rows per second.
words.etymology: Vectorised from vector (Latin vectorem, 'carrier'), referring to SIMD vector registers that carry multiple data values; columnar from Latin columna ('column'); the combined term was standardised by the MonetDB/X100 paper (Boncz, Zukowski, Nes, CIDR 2005) and is now the industry standard label for this execution paradigm.

words.shortDefinition: Three-Phase Commit: extends 2PC with a pre-commit phase to allow non-blocking termination when the coordinator fails.
words.simpleDefinition: Three-phase commit (Skeen, 1981) inserts a pre-commit phase between 2PC's prepare and commit phases. Once a participant receives PRE-COMMIT, it knows every other participant voted yes and can safely commit even if the coordinator crashes. This eliminates 2PC's blocking problem under crash failures — but 3PC is unsafe under network partitions, where two isolated groups can reach conflicting decisions.
words.longDefinition: 2PC's fatal flaw (described in the coordinator-failure problem) is that participants in the PREPARED state cannot unilaterally commit or abort — they must wait for the coordinator's Phase 2 decision, indefinitely if the coordinator fails. 3PC (Dale Skeen, 1981) adds a third state — PRE-COMMITTED — that carries enough information for participants to decide without the coordinator. Phase 1 (Prepare): identical to 2PC — coordinator sends PREPARE; all vote yes or no. Phase 2 (Pre-Commit): coordinator sends PRE-COMMIT to all participants only if all voted yes; participants acknowledge. Phase 3 (Commit): coordinator sends COMMIT; participants apply and release locks. The non-blocking guarantee: if the coordinator crashes after all participants receive PRE-COMMIT, any surviving participant knows (1) all participants voted yes (PRE-COMMIT is only sent after unanimous YES), and (2) no COMMIT has been sent yet. A new coordinator elected from the participants can safely drive the transaction to commit — all pre-committed participants agree. Participants still in PREPARED state (they did not receive PRE-COMMIT) know the coordinator might not have sent PRE-COMMIT to everyone, so they abort — safe because no pre-committed participant can have committed yet. 3PC is non-blocking under crash-recovery failures: a minority of nodes crashing and restarting. It fails under network partitions: if the network splits after some participants receive PRE-COMMIT and others do not, the PRE-COMMITTED partition elects a coordinator that commits while the PREPARED partition elects a coordinator that aborts — split-brain, exactly the atomicity violation 2PC prevents by blocking. Since CAP theorem tells us network partitions occur in real systems, 3PC's non-blocking property comes at an unacceptable price. This is why 3PC was never widely adopted in practice. The correct solution to 2PC's blocking problem is Paxos commit (Gray and Lamport 2004), which tolerates both crash failures and network partitions.
words.connector: Think of 3PC like adding a 'final warning' siren before a building demolition: after the siren, everyone knows demolition is definitely happening (PRE-COMMIT), so even if the demolition foreman disappears, the crew can proceed. But if the siren is heard by only one half of the crew (partition), each half might take a different action — one demolishes, one evacuates — which is worse than both waiting.
words.techContext: The distributed systems textbook exercise of implementing 3PC reveals its partition vulnerability immediately: simulating a network split after the pre-commit broadcast produces two groups that irreconcilably reach commit and abort, corrupting the distributed state.
words.exampleSentence: 3PC solves 2PC's coordinator-failure blocking problem in the theoretical crash-recovery model, but the team's production evaluation showed it was unsafe in their cloud environment where network partitions were more common than outright node crashes.

codeExample.code:
Phase 1 — Prepare:    [identical to 2PC]
  Coordinator → all: PREPARE
  All → Coordinator: VOTE-YES

Phase 2 — Pre-Commit: [new]
  Coordinator → all: PRE-COMMIT
  Participant now knows: all voted YES + commit is safe
  All → Coordinator: ACK-PRE-COMMIT

Phase 3 — Commit:     [identical to 2PC]
  Coordinator → all: COMMIT

COORDINATOR CRASH after Phase 2:
  Surviving participants are all PRE-COMMITTED
  → elect new coordinator → safely commit

NETWORK PARTITION after Phase 2 (3PC failure mode):
  Partition A: PRE-COMMITTED → elects leader → COMMIT
  Partition B: PREPARED     → elects leader → ABORT
  → SPLIT-BRAIN: atomicity violated

words.etymology: Three-Phase Commit is a descriptive name: the protocol has three phases instead of two. Proposed by Dale Skeen in his 1981 Cornell technical report 'Nonblocking Commit Protocols'.

words.shortDefinition: A high-performance LSM-based distributed database compatible with Cassandra's API, rebuilt in C++ for NVMe workloads.
words.simpleDefinition: ScyllaDB is a C++ rewrite of Apache Cassandra that eliminates the JVM and replaces shared-memory threading with a shard-per-core architecture using the Seastar async framework. Each CPU core owns a dedicated partition of data and runs an async event loop — eliminating cross-core locks and garbage collection pauses. P99 write latency is typically 1–2 ms versus 5–10 ms on Cassandra for equivalent hardware.
words.longDefinition: ScyllaDB (Cloudius Systems, 2015; ScyllaDB Inc.) was built on the observation that Apache Cassandra — a Java application on a JVM — was leaving most of the hardware performance of modern NVMe servers on the table. Three specific JVM costs motivated the rewrite: garbage collection pauses (stop-the-world GC events of 50–500 ms routinely pushed Cassandra's p99.9 latency into seconds), thread-per-operation concurrency (Cassandra uses Java threads with blocking I/O, expensive at high parallelism), and cross-core memory contention (Java's shared heap means cores compete for heap memory and CPU cache lines). ScyllaDB's solutions: Seastar framework (an async, non-blocking, single-threaded-per-core C++ framework analogous to Node.js but for systems programming), shard-per-core architecture (each CPU core owns exclusive responsibility for a subset of the token ring, processing reads, writes, compaction, and streaming for its shards on its own thread with no cross-core locking), and io_uring / SPDK for high-throughput NVMe I/O without syscall overhead. The data model and wire protocol are fully compatible with Apache Cassandra (CQL v4, Cassandra-compatible binary protocol) — migration is a drop-in replacement. Storage uses an LSM-tree with a compaction strategy selection similar to Cassandra: SizeTieredCompaction (STCS), LeveledCompaction (LCS), and TimeWindowCompaction (TWCS) for time-series data. TWCS is a ScyllaDB architectural strength: it groups SSTables by time window so that compaction never merges cold historical data with hot recent data, and entire cold SSTables can be deleted in O(1) when their TTL expires without a read-heavy merge. ScyllaDB 5.0 (2022) added Raft-based schema changes — a significant reliability improvement over Cassandra's gossip-based schema propagation, which could produce schema disagreements across nodes. By 2026, ScyllaDB is used at Discord (storing 1 trillion messages), Comcast, and numerous financial services companies where Cassandra's GC pauses were causing SLA violations.

-- Time-series table with TWCS compaction (optimal for ScyllaDB)
CREATE TABLE sensor_readings (
    sensor_id UUID,
    timestamp TIMESTAMP,
    value     DOUBLE,
    PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, timestamp)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (timestamp DESC)
  AND compaction = {
    'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
    'compaction_window_unit': 'HOURS',
    'compaction_window_size': 1
  }
  AND default_time_to_live = 604800;  -- 7-day TTL
